extracted.intended_audience: Researchers designing ML-based science; paper referees and journal editors setting transparency/reproducibility standards
extracted.subtask_description: A consensus checklist and paired guidelines for reporting machine-learning-based scientific studies to ensure validity, reproducibility, and appropriate claims about generalizability. Intended to be used by researchers when designing/implementing studies and by referees and journals when evaluating submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study goals
rubrics_metrics.description: What questions does the study aim to answer? Predictions, interventions, hypotheses?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State the study's primary questions explicitly (e.g., predictive task, causal intervention, hypothesis test). Define outcomes and estimands clearly so that evaluation and claims (prediction vs. causal inference vs. explanation) are aligned with the methods. Avoid overclaiming: do not state causal or generalization conclusions that exceed the study design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computational reproducibility
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide the code, data (or clear data-access instructions), software environment specifications, and random seeds necessary to reproduce results. Include build/run instructions and dependency versions or container images. Note any data or code access restrictions and provide deterministic procedures where possible. Reviewers should verify that sufficient artifacts are available to reproduce key results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data quality
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document data provenance (origins, collection procedures), inclusion/exclusion criteria, and any known biases. Describe missingness (patterns, amount) and how missing data were handled (imputation methods, sensitivity analyses). Report data cleaning steps and justify decisions that affect validity. Watch for selective reporting or undisclosed filtering that could bias results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data preprocessing
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain all preprocessing steps: feature construction, normalization/scaling, encoding of categorical variables, dimensionality reduction, and any transformations. Specify whether preprocessing was fit on training data only and applied to test data to avoid leakage. Provide parameter values and scripts so preprocessing can be inspected and repeated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modeling
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe the model family, architecture, and rationale for model choice. Report hyperparameter ranges, tuning procedures (search algorithm, validation scheme), training protocols (epochs, early stopping), and initialization. Include baselines and justify their selection. Disclose any model selection or post-hoc adjustments to avoid hidden tuning and selective reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data leakage
rubrics_metrics.description: Train-test contamination, target leakage, temporal leakage
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly assess and rule out leakage sources: ensure separation of training/validation/test sets, prevent features constructed from future or target-derived information, and handle temporal or grouped dependencies correctly (e.g., by using time-aware splits or grouping by subject). Describe checks performed to detect leakage. Common pitfalls addressed include train/test contamination, use of leakage-prone features, and hidden hyperparameter tuning that exploits test information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metrics and uncertainty quantification
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose metrics aligned to the scientific question and report them clearly (e.g., calibration and discrimination for prediction, effect sizes for causal claims). Quantify uncertainty using confidence intervals, standard errors, or appropriate resampling methods (bootstrap, cross-validation variance estimation). Avoid cherry-picking favorable metrics; report a prespecified set or justify exploratory analyses and correct for multiple comparisons when necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generalizability and limitations
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State the populations, settings, and time periods to which results are expected to generalize and document known limitations and failure modes. Provide evidence for or against generalization (external validation, holdout populations, sensitivity analyses). Avoid overclaiming broad applicability; transparently discuss domain shifts, subgroup performance, and contexts where the model may fail.
